original_summary: Lost Cities is a two-player card game. Each turn a player plays one card to a strictly ascending colour column (wagers first) or discards it, then draws from the deck or a discard top. Columns cost 20 to open, wagers multiply the result, and there is a bonus for long columns. The previous adaptation, 'Locked Routes', cut it to 3 colours, 2 hands of 16 turns and a secret locked colour.

review.evidence: In the reviewed variation no fixed policy wins. Always-play-slot-1 collects -1 penalties and negative columns. Always-discard scores near 0. Seats alternate first move between hands. Choices clearly change the outcome.

A skilled player beats a careless one. Between competent players, though, the deal decides about 60-70% of matches. Example: W,5,7,9,10 scores 56 while 3,6,9 scores 10, so the deal swings 30-50 points per hand against 5-15 points of decision value. Only about 16 plays per player per match.

Weak players can score, but the strongest levers of the original are missing. There is no voluntary discard, so no hold/dump/feed play. The lock carries little information. This caps how much a strong player can gain over a decent one.

The hidden lock is exposed structurally. With 3 colours and one forbidden, once a player has two columns the lock is known. Any free discard into an empty colour revealed it even earlier. Opponent modelling shrinks to watching public columns.
All scoring is arithmetic on cards in columns and counted penalties.
Turn-based and text-only, using hidden hands and discard piles handled as list operations. 32 rounds, with no board needed.

problems: P1 Deal luck dominates: the high cards and Wagers a player is dealt or draws decide most matches between good players.
P2 Small sample: about 16 plays per player per match from a fresh shuffle each hand.
P3 Wager amplification: a Wager doubles (or more) a column, which magnifies deal luck.
P4 No voluntary discard: the hold / dump / feed-the-opponent decision, central to Lost Cities, is missing.
P5 The hidden lock reveals itself: it is exposed by the second column or the first discard into an empty colour, so there is almost nothing to infer.
P6 Opponent modelling is thin: a player cannot gain by reading the opponent's hidden hand or intentions beyond public columns.

changes.what: Mirrored deal. Hand 1 is shuffled once, and hand 2 reuses exactly the same card order with seats swapped: the player who moved second in hand 1 receives the first player's hand-1 starting cards and moves first. Both players face the same starting hand and the same draw-pile sequence once each.
changes.why: Removes most of the 'who was dealt the 10s and Wagers' difference. What remains is how each player handled the same cards, plus the divergence caused by different discard draws.

changes.what: Two hands of 20 turns (10 plays per player per hand, 40 rounds in total) instead of 16.
changes.why: Gives 20 decisions per player and enough turns to build 5-card columns. Stays within the 40-round limit.

changes.what: A Wager multiplies a positive column score by 1.5 (rounded down) instead of doubling it. Each colour still has only one Wager.
changes.why: Wagers remain a real gamble but no longer swing a hand by 30+ points on their own.

changes.what: Each turn the player chooses a slot AND 'play' or 'discard'. Discarding is free. Only an attempted illegal play costs 1 point and sends the card to the discard pile. Announcements say only 'discarded X', never whether it was voluntary or illegal.
changes.why: Restores the original game's main tactical lever: whether to hold, dump, or avoid feeding the opponent a card they want from the discard pile.

changes.what: The self-lock is replaced by a secret Embargo. At the start of each hand each player secretly names one colour against the OPPONENT. At the end of the hand, the opponent's column in that colour has its score halved (rounded down) if it is positive. All three colours are buildable by everyone.
changes.why: A self-lock with 3 colours is revealed by play. An embargo chosen against the opponent stays hidden: the embargoed player never sees it until scoring. The choice is a real inference. The colours you hold few cards and no high cards in are likely the opponent's strength, so embargo there. The opponent anticipates this and may avoid over-committing to one column. The mirrored deal adds a second-hand layer: you now hold the opponent's hand-1 cards and saw how they used them.
changes.fixes: P5 The hidden lock reveals itself

changes.what: Running totals and penalties stay private until each hand's scoring. Discard draws are announced with the card taken.
changes.why: Each player must infer the opponent's hand from the cards they pick up, the cards they discard and the cards they hold back. That is the opponent-reading of real Lost Cities, now with free discards that can be bluffs or denials.

keeps: Ascending colour columns, with Wagers allowed only before any number card
Play-then-draw turn structure, drawing from the deck or any discard top, but not the card just discarded
Opening cost per column (sum - 8), the multiplier for Wagers, and the long-column bonus
Face-up colour discard piles that feed the opponent

recommendation.reason: The core push-your-luck and denial game is sound and fits the engine. The mirrored deal, free discards and a genuinely hidden embargo fix luck and inference within the limits.

variation.name: Lost Cities: Embargo
variation.summary: A two-player Lost Cities with 3 colours over two mirrored hands of 20 turns. Players build ascending colour columns, can discard freely to dump or deny, and each secretly embargoes one colour of the opponent, which halves that column's score.
variation.rules:
COMPONENTS. A 30-card deck in three colours: Red, Green, Blue. Each colour has number cards 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 and one Wager card. There are three face-up discard piles, one per colour; only the top card of each is visible and takeable. Each player has one column per colour.

STRUCTURE. The match is 2 hands of 20 turns each, 40 rounds in total. A round is one turn of the active player. In hand 1, Seat 1 takes the odd turns (1, 3, ..., 19) and Seat 2 the even turns. In hand 2, Seat 2 takes the odd turns and Seat 1 the even turns.

HAND 1 SETUP (round 1). Shuffle the 30 cards once and record this order as the match order. Deal cards 1-5 to Seat 1 and cards 6-10 to Seat 2. Cards 11-30, in order, form the face-down draw pile (card 11 on top). Each hand is an ordered list of 5 slots; slot 1 is the oldest card.

HAND 2 SETUP (round 21). Clear all columns and discard piles. Do NOT reshuffle. Use the recorded match order: cards 1-5 go to Seat 2 and cards 6-10 go to Seat 1. Cards 11-30 form the draw pile in the same order. Each seat therefore starts hand 2 with the cards the other seat started hand 1 with, and moves at the same position.

EMBARGO (at each hand setup, after the deal). Each player secretly and simultaneously names one colour: Red, Green or Blue. This is their embargo against the opponent for this hand. It is revealed only at end-of-hand scoring.

A TURN. The active player privately sees their own hand. Both players see both players' columns, the tops of the three discard piles, the number of cards in the draw pile, and all earlier announcements of the current hand.
(1) Choose a card by slot, and choose PLAY or DISCARD.
- DISCARD: the card goes face-up onto its colour's discard pile. There is no cost.
- PLAY: if the play is legal, the card is added to the player's column of its colour. If it is illegal, the card goes onto its colour's discard pile and the player loses 1 point.
A number card is legal if it is higher than every number already in that column. A Wager is legal only if that column contains no number card yet.
(2) Choose where to draw from: the draw pile, the Red pile, the Green pile or the Blue pile. The player takes the top card of the chosen pile. If that discard pile is empty, or its top card is the card the player discarded this turn, they take the top card of the draw pile instead. The drawn card goes into slot 5, and the other cards close up to the left. The draw pile always has at least one card at this point.
(3) Announcement to both players: either 'Seat X played [card] to their [colour] column' or 'Seat X discarded [card]'. A discard announcement never says whether it was voluntary or an illegal play. The announcement also gives the pile drawn from, and the card taken if it came from a discard pile. Penalties and totals are not announced.

END OF HAND (after turn 20). Score each of a player's three columns:
- An empty column scores 0.
- Otherwise let S = (sum of its number cards) - 8.
- If S > 0 and the column holds the Wager, multiply S by 1.5 and round down. If S <= 0, the Wager has no effect.
- A column with 5 or more cards, the Wager included, gains +10.
- Embargo: if this column's colour is the one the opponent embargoed, and its score so far is positive, halve it, rounding down. A zero or negative score is unchanged.
The hand score is the sum of the three column scores minus the player's illegal-play penalties for that hand. Add it to the player's total. Then announce both embargoes, both hand scores and both totals.

END OF MATCH. After hand 2 is scored, the match ends.
variation.objective: After both hands, the player with the higher total wins. Equal totals are a draw.
variation.expected_effect: Mirroring means both players start from the same cards and draw-pile sequence, so the gap between them measures play rather than the deal. Expect deal luck to fall from deciding most matches to a minority. The halved Wager keeps the gamble without wild swings. Free, ambiguous discards bring back holding, dumping and denial, and make reading the opponent's hand from their pickups and discards worthwhile. The embargo forces an inference at the start of each hand: guess where the opponent is strong, from the gaps in your own hand. The opponent must hedge between one big column (high payoff, embargo risk) and two medium ones. Simple policies lose. Always discarding scores about 0. Always playing slot 1 bleeds penalties and negative columns. Always drawing from the deck feeds the opponent useful discards unchecked.

balanced.evidence:
SEAT ORDER. Each hand has 16 turns, 8 per player. The first player in a hand moves first; the second takes turn 16 and sees one more round of information. Hand 2 swaps seats (Seat 2 odd turns, Seat 1 even), so over the match each seat moves first once and last once. No structural edge remains.

DRAW PILE. The pile holds 20 cards and at most 16 draws are taken from it per hand, so at least 4 remain and it never runs out. No turn-count asymmetry.

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES, judged by the winner rule.
(a) Always slot 1 + always draw pile. Cards are played in arrival order. A card is often lower than its column's top, so it becomes an illegal discard (-1). Wagers land after numbers and are illegal. High cards close columns early. Typical result: one or two columns with about 2-3 cards and sums near 8-15 (S of about 0-7). Several -1 penalties. Total of about 0-10 per hand. A sensible player who orders cards ascending and wagers early typically builds one column like W,4,6,8,10: S = 28 - 8 = 20, times 2 = 40, plus 10 for 5 cards = 50. Plus a second column of about 5-15. Against sensible play (a) loses almost always. Against random play the two are similar and both outcomes occur.
(b) Always last slot (newest card) + draw pile. Same failure mode as (a); loses to sensible play.
(c) Always draw from a discard pile. Usually redirected to the draw pile because piles are empty, or it takes useless low cards. Not dominant.

NO DOMINANT OPTION.
- Lock choice: best is your weakest colour after seeing 5 cards, which depends on the deal.
- Draw source: depends on what the opponent discarded and whether denial matters.
- Wager timing: early is only good if the colour reaches S > 0. If S <= 0, wagers add nothing but used a turn.

PAYOFF ARITHMETIC. Threshold 8, sums of 0-54 per colour. Positive columns are achievable; scores are consistent with the description.

Both players can realistically win. No policy never loses.

playable.evidence:
LIMITS. steps 14/20, choice steps 3/4 (lock poll + slot + draw source), attributes 15/20, hidden elements 3/3 (hands, deck order, locks), random draws 1/1 (the shuffle at hand setup; later draws take the top of an already-shuffled pile), rounds 32/40. All within limits.

RESOLUTION. Card resolution is fully automatic and ordered: locked colour -> free discard; legal -> column; otherwise discard with -1.
- Legality is defined for numbers and for Wagers.
- An empty column accepts any card (vacuously higher than all numbers; no number present for a Wager).
- The draw fallback covers an empty pile and the just-discarded card. The draw pile can never be empty when needed (minimum 4 left).

LOCKS. The simultaneous lock is a poll.

SCORING. End-of-hand scoring is pure arithmetic on kept numbers.

FINITENESS. Fixed 32 rounds.

No board, judge, clock, trading or conditional block is needed. Two players, so the talk question does not apply. Not an iterated cooperation game.

Minor gap: the rules do not say whether running totals are public. This does not block play.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
SAMPLE SIZE. Each player makes only 8 plays per hand and there are only 2 hands, so the match rests on about 16 plays per player from a 30-card shuffle. Each player sees about 13 of 30 cards per hand.

VARIANCE. Column value is dominated by which high cards (8, 9, 10) and Wagers you are dealt or draw, and the Wager multiplier amplifies it.
- Example: W,5,7,9,10 scores (31-8)x2 + 10 = 56.
- Example: 3,6,9 scores 10.
- Between two competent players the per-hand swing from the deal alone is easily 30-50 points.
- Decisions (lock choice, sequencing, denial draws) are worth perhaps 5-15.
- Estimate: with equal good play, the deal decides about 60-70% of matches. Over just 2 hands, this means chance often decides the winner.

THE HIDDEN LOCK GIVES ALMOST NOTHING TO INFER. Any discard of a colour whose column is empty must be the locked colour, because any card is legal in an empty column. So the first locked discard publicly reveals the lock. Before that, the opponent's columns already show which colours are in use.

OPPONENT MODELLING IS THIN. It reduces to watching public columns and occasionally denying a discard.

NO VOLUNTARY DISCARD. Players cannot discard a playable non-locked card except by taking -1. This removes the original game's main tactical lever (hold vs dump vs feed the opponent).

A skilled player clearly beats a careless one. But between good players the random deal, not reasoning, usually decides the winner.

required_changes: Cut deal luck with a mirrored deal: shuffle once and use the identical card order in hand 2 with seats swapped (Seat 2 receives Seat 1's hand-1 cards and turn positions). Or play 4 hands of 10 turns each (40 rounds) with the same mirroring per pair.
Reduce wager amplification: make a Wager add +50% of S (S x 1.5, rounded down) instead of doubling. Or cap one Wager per column.

Add a voluntary discard: at step (1) the player chooses a slot AND chooses 'play' or 'discard'. Discarding is free; the -1 applies only to an attempted illegal play. This restores the hold/dump/feed decisions and the denial game.

Make the lock genuinely hidden: since discards are free under the change above, a discard no longer reveals the lock. Or reveal only 'card discarded' without saying whether it was a locked or illegal discard, and keep running totals private until the hand ends.

Give the lock a payoff to reason about. For example, at end of hand a player scores +1 per card of the opponent's locked colour that the player holds in columns, or +5 if the player correctly names the opponent's lock in a final simultaneous guess. This creates real inference about the opponent's hidden choice.

balanced.evidence:
COLUMN SCORE RANGE. Each colour's numbers 2-10 sum to 54.
- Best possible column: W+2..10 = (54-8)=46, x1.5 = 69, +10 = 79; embargoed, 39.
- Typical strong column 6,7,9,10: S = 24; with the Wager 36; at 5 cards +10 = 46; embargoed, 23.
- Weak column '2' alone: -6. Weak column '3,5': 0.
A sensible hand (two committed colours, a third dumped or used lightly) scores about 40-70.

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES, by the WINNER RULE (higher total):
(a) Always DISCARD, always draw from the pile: 0 per hand, 0 total.
- Against sensible play (about +40 to +70 per hand): LOSES every time.
- Against random play (about half of random plays are illegal, -1 each, and low cards start columns that end negative): often wins.
- It loses to sensible play, so it is not a never-lose policy.
(b) Always PLAY slot 1 (oldest card): each colour's column becomes the running-record subsequence of the cards that arrive. That is about 2-3 records per colour, sum about 18-22, S about 10-14 per colour. With about 8-12 illegal plays at -1, the hand totals about 15-30.
- Against sensible play: LOSES.
- Against random play: usually wins.
(c) Always PLAY slot 5 (newest card): same structure as (b), about 15-30 per hand, loses to sensible play.
(d) Always draw from a discard pile: this only helps when the top card fits a column. Blind, it recycles junk and does no better than (a) or (b).

STRICT DOMINANCE. No option is strictly better whatever the opponent does.
- An illegal PLAY is strictly worse than DISCARD (same card movement, -1). That is an error trap, not a dominant option.
- Embargo is a 3x3 guess. The cell 'embargo hits the opponent's largest positive column' costs them about 10-25 points; the other cells cost 0-5. The best colour depends on the opponent's hand and plan, so no colour dominates.

SEAT EDGE. In hand 1 Seat 1 moves first and draws card 11 first. Hand 2 swaps the starting hands (cards 1-5 and 6-10) and the move order on the same deck order, so each seat plays each position once. The swap is not an exact duplicate, because draws depend on choices, but the systematic order and deal edge is cancelled.

HAND-2 INFORMATION. Each player already knows the opponent's hand-2 starting hand (they held it in hand 1) and the deck cards they themselves drew. That is roughly the cards the opponent will now draw, and it is symmetric. Neither seat gains an information edge.

Both players can realistically win. This is not a cooperation game, so the 'higher total' cooperation test does not apply.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
CHANCE IS LIMITED. Chance enters only through one shuffle. Hand 2 reuses the same order with starting hands and seats swapped, which cancels most deal luck. The remaining luck is divergence in which pile cards each player ends up drawing, about 10-20% of the outcome.

WHAT THERE IS TO INFER:
- Opponent hand contents, from their plays, discards and discard-pile pickups. An announced discard may hide an illegal play.
- The opponent's main colours, which drives the embargo guess and the denial of useful discards.
- In hand 2, the remembered deck order, the opponent's starting hand and the cards they drew in hand 1. This rewards memory and planning: you know roughly what the opponent will draw.

WHAT THERE IS TO PLAN:
- Which colours to commit to, given that a column costs -8.
- When to lay the Wager, which must come before any number.
- Reaching 5 cards for +10.
- Avoiding feeding the opponent useful discards.
- Hedging against the embargo by spreading value.

WHEN BOTH PLAY WELL. The mirrored deal makes the totals close, and the result is decided by better tracking, embargo prediction and discard denial, not by the draw alone. A reasoning player clearly beats a slot-order or random player: roughly 50+ versus 15-30 per hand.
